 Home » Mexico GP FP3 telemetry: Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes in close fight for pole Mexico GP FP3 telemetry: Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes in close fight for pole
 The battle for pole position at the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix looks extraordinarily close, with Mexico GP FP3 telemetry suggesting that McLaren holds a marginal advantage over Ferrari and Mercedes. However, Charles Leclerc and Andrea Kimi Antonelli could still make the difference through their driving, while Max Verstappen remains a potential contender despite Red Bull’s apparent difficulties.
 The final practice session produced an exceptionally tight competitive picture, with at least five drivers appearing capable of challenging for pole position. What makes the situation particularly interesting is how differently the leading cars generate their lap times. Some have clear strengths in individual sectors and equally noticeable weaknesses elsewhere, yet their overall performances converge towards almost identical lap times.
 Qualifying therefore looks likely to be decided by thousandths of a second, with even small changes in track conditions potentially becoming decisive. McLaren appears to have the most complete package, but Ferrari’s braking performance and Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s ability to exploit the Mercedes could make the final result difficult to predict.
 Mexico GP FP3 telemetry reveals an exceptionally close qualifying battle
 The data from final practice highlights how different technical characteristics can produce remarkably similar lap times. Rather than one car holding a consistent advantage around the entire Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the leading teams appear to be gaining and losing performance in different parts of the circuit.
 This creates a particularly uncertain situation ahead of Q3. A driver who performs exceptionally well through the high-speed corners could still lose that advantage under braking or through the slower sections, while another car might recover the deficit through superior traction and kerb handling.
 The result is an unusually open contest in which the smallest differences in tyre preparation, driving precision and circuit conditions could determine the starting order. The contrasting strengths of the leading cars make the earlier Ferrari telemetry findings from Mexico FP2 particularly relevant when assessing how the competitive picture has developed.
 Mercedes changes setup as Andrea Kimi Antonelli compensates for car limitations
 One of the most interesting developments concerns Mercedes, which appears to have made a significant setup change compared with Friday. The team seems to have adopted a considerably softer mechanical configuration, potentially sacrificing some front-end grip to reduce overheating of the rear tyres.
 That compromise could be particularly important over a race distance, where excessive rear-tyre temperatures may become a decisive limitation. The revised setup has also noticeably improved the Mercedes’ ability to ride the kerbs, although the car still appears to have some weaknesses through the faster sections during longer runs.
 Surprisingly, however, those limitations seem to disappear when the car is fitted with fresh soft tyres. The telemetry suggests that Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s driving is especially important in extracting the available performance over a single qualifying lap.
 The Italian driver uses the grip offered by the new tyres to compensate for the car’s limitations, carrying substantial speed through the circuit’s sweeping high-speed sequence, commonly known as the snake. His aggressive approach allows him to cut through the corners while maintaining momentum, helping Mercedes remain among the leading contenders.
 The impression is not necessarily that Mercedes has the fastest car overall. Instead, Andrea Kimi Antonelli appears capable of compensating for its front-end limitations in the high-speed sections through his driving technique.
 Whether the Italian can reproduce that performance during qualifying, when finding the absolute limit becomes essential, will be one of the key questions heading into Q3.
 McLaren appears strongest overall as Ferrari loses performance in fast corners
 Based on the telemetry, McLaren currently appears to have the most complete car. The Woking team’s package performs well in both slow and high-speed corners, while also demonstrating an impressive ability to attack the kerbs through the stadium section.
 The main area where McLaren continues to concede some performance to its rivals is braking. Nevertheless, its overall compromise appears to be the most effective, potentially giving the team a very slight advantage in the fight for pole position.
 Even so, the differences are measured in thousandths of a second, leaving very little separating the leading contenders.
 Ferrari, meanwhile, appears less complete than it did during the first two practice sessions. The SF-26 continues to perform extremely well through slow corners, during acceleration and over the kerbs, but it now seems to struggle more noticeably in the faster sections.
 The weakness is particularly evident through the snake, where the Italian car appears to lack some lateral grip. This contrasts with McLaren, which seems better equipped to maintain performance across the circuit’s different corner types.
 The impression is that Ferrari may have moved further towards a softer mechanical setup, prioritising slow-speed performance and the ability to absorb kerbs. However, that decision appears to come at a significant cost through the high-speed corners.
 This represents another example of the distinctive setup challenges facing the Ferrari SF-26 in Mexico , where finding an effective compromise between aerodynamic and mechanical grip is particularly difficult.
 Charles Leclerc’s braking performance remains Ferrari’s biggest strength
 Despite the apparent high-speed limitations, Ferrari retains one particularly important advantage: braking performance. Charles Leclerc continues to extract a substantial part of his lap time in the circuit’s most demanding braking zones, where the SF-26 appears especially competitive.
 This creates an almost opposite performance profile compared with McLaren. While the British team appears to possess the more balanced package across the lap, Ferrari is particularly effective under braking and through slower sections, compensating for some of the time lost in faster corners.
 The two cars therefore arrive at very similar overall lap times despite exhibiting distinctly different characteristics. That contrast could become especially important in qualifying, where even a small variation in braking precision or cornering speed could alter the final order.
 The significance of these differences can also be explored through the F1 qualifying telemetry and corner comparison tool, which examines braking behaviour, corner speeds and acceleration patterns once qualifying lap data becomes available.
 Why Ferrari may struggle to improve on soft tyres in Mexico qualifying
 Another interesting indication concerns the relationship between the medium and soft tyre compounds. Ferrari appears to have a more similar balance on the two compounds, whereas its rivals seem considerably more rear-biased when running on the mediums.
 When the softer compound is fitted, the additional front-end grip helps those cars compensate for that imbalance during a qualifying lap. Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s performance provides a particularly clear example of how this can work.
 This could explain why Ferrari has appeared to find it more difficult to improve its lap times when switching to the softest available compound. If the SF-26 is already relatively well balanced on the medium tyre, the transition to the soft may not deliver the same improvement in handling experienced by its competitors.
 However, that remains an interpretation of the available data rather than a confirmed conclusion. It will be especially interesting to see whether the same behaviour emerges during qualifying, when the drivers push to extract the maximum performance from fresh soft tyres.
 Red Bull struggles with setup, but Max Verstappen remains a pole threat
 Red Bull appears to have taken a small step backwards, with the car still struggling to find the ideal compromise for the Mexican circuit. Based on the performance demonstrated so far, the team does not currently appear to have the package required to be considered the favourite for pole position.
 Nevertheless, excluding Max Verstappen from the fight would be premature. The Dutch world champion has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to make the difference during decisive moments, meaning his individual performance could still influence the outcome even if Red Bull’s underlying pace appears less convincing.
 With such narrow margins separating the leading contenders, a particularly strong qualifying lap could be enough to change the expected order.
 Mexico GP pole position could be decided by thousandths of a second
 The overall picture points towards an extremely unpredictable qualifying session, with five drivers, and potentially more, capable of challenging for first place on the grid.
 McLaren appears to have the most balanced car, Mercedes is benefiting from Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s ability to overcome its limitations, and Ferrari remains especially competitive under braking thanks to Charles Leclerc. Red Bull has shown less convincing performance, but Max Verstappen cannot be ruled out.
 With the gaps so small, even a one-degree change in track temperature, slightly better tyre preparation or a single perfectly executed corner could shift the competitive balance.
 After three practice sessions, the leading teams remain separated by remarkably little. The decisive factor may ultimately be the drivers’ ability to extract everything from their cars when qualifying reaches its most demanding moments, with the battle for pole position in Mexico potentially decided by mere thousandths of a second.
